query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For cast equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-/medium-entropy alloy, the temperature- and strain-rate-dependent mechanical response is governed by a competition between perfect-dislocation glide and deformation nanotwinning that is set by the temperature-dependent intrinsic stacking-fault energy (SFE). Low temperature (≤200 K) and/or high plastic-strain rates (≥10² s⁻¹) lower the effective SFE felt by moving partials and suppress dynamic recovery, so the critical stress for twin nucleation is reached early, producing a high twin volume fraction that raises the strain-hardening rate and flow stress while delaying necking. At elevated temperature (≥600 K) or quasi-static rates (≤10⁻³ s⁻¹) the higher SFE and longer time for thermally activated cross-slip favour full dislocation glide with little twinning, giving lower work-hardening and strength. Hence the density of deformation twins acts as the structural mediator that continuously links test temperature/strain rate to the observed dynamic mechanical behaviour.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy produced by vacuum induction melting and casting, homogenised 1 h @ 1200 °C, water-quenched, single-phase FCC, grain size 20–40 µm, <0.05 wt % interstitials, no prior cold work.
generation.intervention: Vary testing temperature (77 K, 298 K, 673 K) and true strain rate (10⁻³ s⁻¹, 10⁰ s⁻¹, 10³ s⁻¹) in uniaxial compression/tension while keeping chemistry, grain size and surface finish fixed.
generation.conditions: Tests performed in inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; strain to at least 30 % to reach steady work-hardening; adiabatic heating monitored (thermocouples + high-speed IR).
generation.structural_mediator: Deformation twin volume fraction (and associated stacking faults) quantified by post-mortem EBSD/TEM and, in situ, by synchrotron X-ray diffraction peak-broadening.
generation.mechanism: Lower SFE at low T and high   strain rate promotes nucleation of Shockley partials on successive {111} planes, creating twin embryos that thicken into nanotwins. Twins subdivide grains (dynamic Hall–Petch), block dislocation motion and raise the strain-hardening rate. As T rises or strain-rate falls, higher SFE and greater time for cross-slip favour perfect-dislocation glide, giving fewer twins, lower strain-hardening and earlier localisation.
generation.predicted_outcome: 1. Flow stress at 10 % true strain will increase by ≈30 % when temperature drops from 298 K to 77 K at 10³ s⁻¹. 2. At a fixed 298 K, increasing strain rate from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 10³ s⁻¹ will raise the average twin fraction from <1 % to >10 %, accompanied by a ~25 % jump in strain-hardening rate. 3. Above 600 K the twin fraction will remain below 1 % irrespective of strain rate, and rate sensitivity will be negligible.
generation.baseline: Room-temperature quasi-static (10⁻³ s⁻¹) response: 0.2 % proof stress ≈300 MPa, uniform elongation ≈40 %, negligible deformation twins.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis expected to hold for grain sizes 5–100 µm, single-phase FCC condition, and compositions within ±2 at % of equiatomic FeNiCrMn. It may not apply if grains are nanocrystalline (<1 µm) or if additional elements (e.g., Al, C) alter SFE by >20 mJ m⁻² or introduce other phases.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitude of SFE change with temperature for this alloy is not yet measured; predicted strength increments are approximate. Adiabatic heating at high strain rate could partially offset the low-temperature benefit, adding experimental scatter.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (A) baseline FeNiCrMn; (B) FeNiCrMn+2 at % Al (raises SFE by ~20 mJ m⁻²). Test both under identical conditions at 77 K & 298 K, 10³ s⁻¹. Characterise twin fraction post-mortem and in situ hardening behaviour.
measurements: True stress–strain curves up to 30 % strain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (i) twin volume fraction does NOT correlate with increased flow stress/strain-hardening across the temperature/strain-rate matrix (e.g., high strength measured without increased twinning, or abundant twins without strength increase); OR (ii) raising SFE with Al addition fails to suppress twinning and the associated strength jump at low T/high rate.
